quick.summary: Why beautiful prototypes fail early tests, and how to get better feedback.
quick.takeaway: Test simple boxes first. Polish invites arguments about surface details instead of flow.

beats.line: Users only argued about button colors during my test. What went wrong?
Think of building a house. You check blueprints before painting the walls.
Because moving a painted wall is very expensive.
Exactly. But you showed them a fully painted room.
When things look polished, people focus on the surface details.
Designers call this going high fidelity too early.
Can I just say it looks too real too soon?
Yes. Too real too soon. Keep it rough to test the core idea.
So I should test simple gray boxes first to see if the flow works.
You will get feedback on how it works, not how it looks.

quiz.question: Why is it better to use unpolished gray boxes for early concept testing?
options: It forces users to focus on the structure and flow.
It saves storage space on your computer.
It proves to stakeholders that you are working fast.
It prevents engineers from building it too quickly.
quiz.explanation: Simple visuals prevent distraction, ensuring you get feedback on the idea itself.

quiz.question: A fully polished prototype guarantees better early feedback from users.
quiz.explanation: If it looks finished, users will critique superficial things like fonts and colors instead of the core logic.
